newsitem.title: USA: U.S. downplays European concerns over new soybeans.
newsitem.headline: U.S. downplays European concerns over new soybeans.

text.p: U.S. soybean sales to Europe will be down this year, but not because of consumer fears of new genetically engineered soybeans, Agriculture Department officials and trade analysts said Monday.
"To attribute the decline of exports in anything to any one factor is ludicrous," said Paul Drazek, senior trade advisor to Agriculture Secretary Dan Glickman.

Drazek made his comments on the eve of the arrival of the season's first shipment into Europe of newly harvested soybeans from the United States, which for the first time may include some genetically-modified crop.

Consumer activist Jeremy Rifkin has launched an aggressive campaign against the new product, and said Monday that he and others may stage a demonstration at the port of Hamburg, Germany, to protest the arrival of the shipment.
"This is a major trade confrontation. This is not going to go away," Rifkin said in an interview. "European consumers will not take genetically engineered soybeans."

Rifkin alleged that U.S. soybean sales to Europe have dropped "by at least 10 percent" or $150 million worth because of Europe's concern over the soybeans. The soybeans were developed by agribusiness giant Monsanto Co. and grown commercially for the first time this year by U.S. farmers.
Estimates are that about two percent of the new U.S. soybean crop contains the so-called transgenic soybeans.

Rifkin, who has been working to organise a consumer boycott of the soybeans in Europe, said that consumer response has been unexpectedly strong, and noted that some European soybean buyers have begun to cancel orders for U.S. soybeans due to consumer backlash.
Administration officials were sceptical of Rifkin's claims that the consumer worries have cut sales.
"You can't rule out the impacts of genetically engineered soybeans, but I think it's a minor influence at this point," said a senior Agriculture Department analyst.

U.S. trade experts pointed to a big European feed grains crop, high soybean prices earlier in the year, a slow U.S. soybean harvest this year and changes in Europe's agricultural policy as reasons for the lower purchases of U.S. soybeans.

According to the Agriculture Department, U.S. soybean sales booked to the European Union currently total 1.6 million metric tons, down 15 percent from last year's 1.925 million. Accumulated soybean exports to Europe this year total 959,500 tons, down more than 30 percent from 1.47 million last year.

Experts said the numbers were not surprising, and have little to do with the new gene modified soybeans. They said the trend of lower U.S. soybean purchases by Europe started in the late 1980s. Europe last year bought 8.9 million tons of U.S. soybeans, down from 10.1 million the previous year.

Officials and others were sceptical that recent announcements by some European soybean users that they would not use the new gene-modified soybeans in some products would significantly decrease U.S. soybean exports.
"It's not clear that this will cause any loss in soybean sales," said Tim Galvin, Associate Administrator of the Agriculture Department's Foreign Agricultural Service.

Galvin rejected calls from Rifkin and other biotech critics that the genetically altered soybeans be separated from regular soybeans and labelled. "As a practical matter, it's impossible to separate these products," he said.
